title: Domain-specific health-care trust is associated with care seeking and care avoidance
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 32028 revised April 2026; nationally representative U.S. adult survey with trust, care-seeking, and mechanism measures
geography: United States; adult respondents and health-care entities including doctors, nurses, hospitals, insurers, and public-health authorities

observations.period: January 2024 paper; revised April 2026; survey fielding and analytic period are study-defined

denominator.unit: nationally representative U.S. adult survey; respondent count and individual scenario universes are not stated in the official abstract

care_seeking.value: Higher trust in the health-care system is strongly associated with greater retrospective and anticipated preventive and elective care-seeking and lower care avoidance

relative_magnitude.value: The reported association is comparable in magnitude to gradients associated with education and income

trust_composition.value: Trust components are relatively substitutable across health-care entities, while within-domain components are more complementary, especially among individual providers

entity_difference.value: Counterfactual trust losses have different predicted behavioral consequences, with trust in doctors playing the largest role in the reported simulations

heterogeneity.value: The relationship differs by age and political affiliation; the paper reports no differential relationship for Black respondents

observations.method: Nationally representative U.S. survey guided by a theoretical model in which care-seeking depends on perceived usefulness, expected disutility, out-of-pocket costs, and claim denials; the paper measures overall and entity-specific trust, retrospective and prospective care-seeking, and mechanism variables, with structural estimates and counterfactual simulations.
observations.uncertainty: The source is primarily survey and model evidence: association does not establish that a trust change caused a later care decision. Anticipated care-seeking is not realized treatment, completion, health improvement, affordability, or durable trust. Structural estimates depend on the model and measured beliefs; the official abstract does not provide a full denominator or all fielding details.
observations.subgroup: Adult respondents; trust in the overall system, doctors, nurses, hospitals, insurers, CDC, and other public-health entities; age, political affiliation, race, income, and education comparisons; preventive, elective, vaccination, and other study-defined care scenarios.
observations.counterinterpretation: People who expect better care, face fewer barriers, or have more resources may both report greater trust and seek care more often. Trust can be a proxy for prior experience or access, and lower care seeking may reflect appropriate choice, cost, time, transportation, provider availability, or health status rather than distrust alone.

related_sources.claim: Revised official NBER paper PDF and abstract context.
Pre-registration associated with the survey study.

boundary: This record adds a trust-to-care-seeking and care-avoidance pathway. It does not establish a causal trust shock, realized treatment, affordability, health outcome, patient-provider encounter, remedy, durable trust change, or political action.
